author: Lindsay McCabe
title: Changes to coronial legislation to broaden next-of-kin determinations
content:
Readers please be advised that this article mentions First Nations people who have passed away, including children.




On Tuesday 22nd September 2026, the Minns Labor Government announced changes to the 

Coroners Act 2009

 NSW, specifically, the section of the legislation that instructs coroners to determine and appoint a Senior Next-of-Kin. This followed a statutory review of the Act, and is in response to one of the many recommendations made by the review. 




When a person’s death is reported to the coroner, a Senior Next-of-Kin is appointed. The Senior Next-of-Kin has the exclusive authority to make decisions regarding the person who has died while they are in the care of the coroner. For example, the Senior Next-of-Kin can object to a post-mortem examination being conducted. Being appointed Senior Next-of-Kin also means that the coroner has an obligation to provide mandatory notifications about the progress of a coronial investigation to the Senior Next-of-Kin. When, where and how a person is laid to rest is also under the authority of the Senior Next-of-Kin. 




Who is appointed as Senior Next-of-Kin is decided by a strict legal framework. The 

Coroners Act 2009

 (NSW) s 6A states that the Senior Next-of-Kin must be the deceased person’s spouse or de facto partner; if they have no spouse or de facto partner, then any of the adult children of the deceased person can be appointed. If the person has no adult children, then the person’s parent/s may be appointed. 




This appointment-flow hierarchy has been problematic for Mob for many years, across many jurisdictions. It does not take into account our kinship systems, laws, or spiritual beliefs. One of the earliest challenges of the Senior Next-of-Kin hierarchy involved 

two Aboriginal parents

 who could not agree on where to bury their deceased adult child. The mother wanted to hold a Catholic ceremony and burial in Darwin; the father however wanted to have a burial on their homelands, Bardi Country, and provided the Court with supporting information outlining the cultural obligations to do so. The Court ruled in favour of the mother. 




In 

2016

, the NSW Supreme Court was asked to rule on a matter where the Senior Next-of-Kin appointment had been challenged. In this matter, the coroner had appointed a deceased man’s de facto partner as the Senior Next-of-Kin, as per the legislation. This allowed the partner, a Gumbaynggirr woman, to make arrangements for the deceased man’s burial to take place in Bowraville. The man’s sister however, wanted the man to be taken home to Weilwan Country and to be buried alongside his ancestors. The Court ruled in favour of the man’s de facto partner, citing common law precedent. Further, because the de facto partner of the deceased man established her de facto status to the Court, she held ‘administrative priority’; in other words, she had the highest right as per the legislation. 




More recently, in 2024, the Supreme Court of NSW decided on a dispute between a deceased man’s de facto partner and mother who could not agree on where to bury him. The de facto partner of the man insisted he wanted to be buried in La Parouse; his mother wanted to take him home to his father in Cherbourg, Wakka Wakka Country, where he could be buried on Country. The Court held in favour of the man’s de facto partner, accepting that she was the deceased man’s de facto partner at the time of his death. 




So, who is appointed Senior Next-of-Kin when a person dies has significant ramifications for where, when, and how a person is returned to Country. 




There have however been instances where the appointment of Senior Next-of-Kin has affirmed cultural responsibilities and laws, albeit outside of NSW. In 

1999

, the non-Aboriginal spouse of a deceased Aboriginal man sought to bury them in Port Augusta. The deceased man’s father wished to bury him in Oodnadatta, where other members of the family had been buried, and on Yankintatjara Country. Several affidavits were presented to the Court, highlighting that, according to cultural responsibilities and practices, the head of the family should be empowered to make these decisions, not the spouse. The deceased’s spouse, on the other hand, argued that the children of the deceased would not be able to visit their father’s grave if it were located 700kms away in Oodnadatta. Significantly, the Court ruled in favour of the father of the deceased man, allowing him to take his son home, and to be buried according to Aboriginal law and custom.  




The announcement by the Minns Labor government then is a welcome one indeed. It was sparked by a completely different issue, though. As we have seen, when a person dies, and in particular where there is no will, the legislation states that the person’s spouse or de facto partner holds administrative priority, and so is often appointed as Senior Next-of-Kin. Unfortunately, this too often means that for women who have experienced domestic violence at the hands of their partner, that partner is very likely to be appointed as Senior Next-of-Kin, and can therefore make decisions about the laying to rest of the deceased. 




Advocacy by the parents and families

 of women who have died, and who have had an abusive partner appointed as Senior Next-of-Kin, have campaigned for the legislation to be amended for years. This is a necessary change, and one that gives the coroner the power to appoint a different Senior Next-of-Kin in cases where there is family and/or domestic violence. This is a really, really important outcome/change, and one that will allow families to focus on their grief instead of fighting for the right to lay their person to rest. 




In the 

media release,

 the Minns Labor government noted the ‘changes regarding senior next of kin appointments will also recognise extended familial or kinship structures among different cultures such as Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities’. As briefly shown here, and with 

plenty of evidence elsewhere

, this is something that we have been arguing for for many years. Had successive governments listened to us, perhaps the families who advocated for this change would not have had to. 




Despite the Minns Labor government’s pretense that they had Mob in mind all along, this reform was never about us, or it would have been done years ago. There has been little information about how the legislation will be amended to recognise our kinship systems or laws, or what criteria coroners will use in their application of this reform. With our collective lived experiences, it is perhaps right to be cautious of another government reform, particularly one that includes us 

after

 the fact.




This doesn’t take away from the benefits that these reforms will have for families when their person dies, and for whom an abuser has been granted all the rights of Senior Next-of-Kin. The advocacy of the families who fought for this, through their grief and their trauma, is applauded. Achieving this kind of reform is momentous. As many of us have been saying all along, though, 

if you get it right for Mob, you get it right for everyone

.
